```text
launcher: env DM_LANG=zh-Hant (saved choice)
launcher: env DM_METAL_HUD=1 (saved choice)
[dm] cheats: ~/Library/Application Support/nxnative/0100F2C0115B6000/cheats: no file for build 5CB42B1CF25469FB
[dm] [nvn] present tick 60 Hz, interval mode game (original semantics) (game profile present_interval; present interval set by the game 1; window, fixed 60 Hz)
[dm] [nvn] the game sets present interval 1 → 2
[dm] [nvn] power up to frame 600: CPU energy 1.66 W, 27.7 mJ per frame (60.0 fps)
[dm] [nvn] power up to frame 900: CPU energy 1.64 W, 27.3 mJ per frame (60.0 fps)
[dm] [nvn] power up to frame 1200: CPU energy 1.58 W, 26.4 mJ per frame (60.0 fps)
[dm] [nvn] power up to frame 1500: CPU energy 1.58 W, 26.8 mJ per frame (59.0 fps)
[dm] [nvn] power up to frame 1800: CPU energy 1.54 W, 25.7 mJ per frame (60.0 fps)
```

No `frame step` line: the 1.4.2 main has no state page.

### Fork patches line

```text
fork patches: runtime-profile,ios-game-data-folder,ios-slim-ipa,nsp-dotnet-home,nsp-chain-changed-note,nsp-work-dir,bc-cpu-decode,mac-keymap,mac-library-folder,hades2-update-profile,env-switches-verify,ios-probe,fork-docs,ref-hle-hid-d2r,fork-patches-stamp,nsp-dotnet-root-verify,games-md-gallery,cheats-engine,cheats-mac-panel,front-mac-enter-fullscreen-once-the-app-is-activ,front-mac-dm-screen
```

### Screenshots and performance numbers

60.0 fps with the problem; 30.0 fps at the right speed with the fix below.

### A proposed fix, tested locally

The place to fix it looks like `derive_profile`, not the host: many profiles set `fps_target 60` with no frame step stubs and rely on the cap alone, so the host cannot simply drop the cap when there is no state page. Only the five profiles whose `patches.py` has `FRAME_STEP` (Tears of the Kingdom, Breath of the Wild, and three others) depend on stubs for one build.

The change: when the profile's `patches.py` has `FRAME_STEP` stubs, and none of them is for the derived version's main, the derived profile gets `fps_target 0` (the game's own step), with a comment saying why. The table is read with `ast`, without running the file. Registered builds and `shader_only` derivations are unchanged. Profiles without `FRAME_STEP` are unchanged. About 17 lines in `scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py`, plus a test in `dm/tools/tests/test_nsp_incremental.py`.

What I checked:

- The new test fails without the change (`'60' != '0'`) and passes with it. `test_nsp_incremental` (42), `test_nsp_alias` (4) and `test_nsp_mac_app` (44) all pass.
- `derive_profile` on this game's real 1.4.2 files writes `fps_target 0` and the comment.
- I built the Mac host from that profile (`DM_GAME_FPS_TARGET 0`) and the settings list (no Frame rate row any more), put them into an APFS clone of the built app, and ran it with no environment overrides for 70 s: `the game sets present interval 1 → 2`, then 30.0 fps in every power line, game time at real speed. The old saved choice `DM_FPS_TARGET=30` was not applied, as the new settings list no longer offers it.
- Not checked: an iPhone build, a full rebuild through the launcher, `scripts/regress.py check` (the change only reaches derived profiles of the five `FRAME_STEP` games).

Since the script is vendored from seedds/nxnative, I'd send the change there as a PR, per CONTRIBUTING's upstream-first rule. Would you take that change? If so, I'll open the PR and link it here.

body:
Players want to see which games NX2Apple supports, including games they do not own yet. #281 showed these games as cards in the library. That mixed the player's own games with a catalogue. It also made the launcher slow: every redraw built 150 cards instead of 30 (see the performance test from #298). The list gets its own page instead, a Store.

## What the Store shows

- Every game the engine has a profile for, as one light row per game. A row has the name, the cover if one is cached, whether the game is verified, and the update version it needs.
- A search field at the top.
- Tapping a game shows what the player needs to play it: the base game, the update version, DLC if any, and notes such as "60 fps with 1.9.0".
- A game the player owns is marked. Tapping it opens the game in the library.

## Where the data comes from

The data comes from the game profiles in the engine tree (`dm/games`). The engine ships by release (#227), so the list changes with an engine update and needs no app release.

## Limits

- The library shows only owned games.
- The rows are built lazily. Opening the Store is a new interaction in `LauncherPerformanceTests` and stays within its budget.
- Buttons use the shared control sizes (`LauncherControl`), and no label wraps, in every language.

## Starting point

`SupportedGames` in #281 already loads the profiles. It leaves #281 together with the "All" filter. Its last version is in commit e4befb15 on `feat/launcher-roundup`.

## Open question

Does the Store also appear in console mode, and how does a controller move through it?
title: Launcher: a Store page that lists every supported game

### Idea

Breath of the Wild on the Mac is capped at 60 fps and at the game's own 1080p output. seedds/nxnative#76 lets a Breath of the Wild 1.9.0 build run above 60 fps and render above 1080p. `DM_FPS_TARGET` 61 to 240 gives a variable frame step. `DM_RENDER_SCALE` above 1.0 works on the Mac only. body:
### Idea

**Route C M5: signing, packaging and incremental builds for the shell, broken-framework tolerance and docs.**

Follows M4 (#270) and #226. From `docs/launcher-c-plan.md`:
- **Signing order and self-check:** frameworks signed first (no entitlements), then the shell executable with `increased-memory-limit`, then the shell bundle, followed by `codesign --verify --strict`, `otool -l` (`LC_ID_DYLIB`, `LC_RPATH`) and `plutil` checks before install.
- **Incremental packaging:** cache each signed framework per game and never re-sign an unchanged one, so adding a game or changing the shell rewrites only what changed. Measure the time for "add a second game" and for the 7-day re-sign.
- **Re-signing keeps everything:** re-signing or updating the shell installs over the existing app, so `Documents` (game data, saves, bookmarks) survives. Verified on a device for the free 7-day account and a paid team.
- **Broken-framework tolerance:** a framework whose chain, title ID or sections do not match is marked broken in its own row, the other games still play.
- **FH gate:** decide and test the `loader: FH` games (the plan's FH path) before they can be added to the shell.
- **Docs:** the player's README and the launcher's help describe the one-app install, re-signing, adding and removing games.
- Device checks on iOS 26 and 27.

**Done when:** a shell with two or more games re-signs in place without touching the data, adding a game re-signs only the new framework and the shell, a broken framework only breaks its own row, and the docs explain it.

### Outcome

The one-app install is as robust as the per-game IPAs today, re-signing is quick and never touches game data, and players have documentation for it.
title: Route C M5: signing, packaging, incremental builds and broken-framework tolerance

body:
### Idea

**Route C M4: per-game data, settings, external drive and DLC in the shell.**

The shell (one app for all games, #226) now installs from the launcher, shows the library and starts Breath of the Wild from its framework on a real iPhone, with the game data in `Documents/games/<title ID>/`. M3 (a second game in the same shell) is being checked now. This issue is the next milestone from `docs/launcher-c-plan.md`, kept separate so #226 can finish.

What M4 covers:
- **Isolated data per game:** `Documents/games/<id>/{romfs.img, romfs/, save, temp, msl, pso, aoc}` for every title, with no shared state between games.
- **External drive:** a per-title bookmark for game data on a USB drive or SSD (`pickedDataBookmark.<title ID>`, with migration from the per-game app's key), a stale bookmark falling back to `Documents`, and an identity check (`romfs_identity` from the manifest) that falls back on a mismatch instead of loading the wrong data.
- **DLC:** `DM_AOC_DIR` per game, `aoc/<index>.img` or folders mounting in the game, and the launcher copying the DLC next to the game data.
- **Per-game overrides:** `DM_MSL_DIR` and `DM_PSO_BUNDLE` from the game's folder first, then app-wide, `DM_PROFILE` per game, as in the plan's environment table.
- The library never treats a data file as "game installed" (only a framework is).

**Done when:** two titles on one device have isolated data, settings and saves, a stale bookmark and an identity mismatch both fall back cleanly, and a game with DLC mounts it.

### Outcome

Several games in one app behave as if each were its own app: their own data, saves, DLC and settings, with game data allowed on an external drive.
title: Route C M4: per-game data, settings, external drive and DLC in the shell

body:
### Idea

**A project domain with a static landing page and a download host on Cloudflare (R2), for the engine-update plan in #227 and #267.**

Today a player finds the project through the GitHub README and downloads from GitHub Releases. With the plan agreed in #227 (the release carries the engine, players update by version, an experimental engine channel), the launcher reads a signed `latest.json` and downloads the app and engine zips from an ordered list of sources. GitHub stays the first source. This issue adds a second home that we control:

1. **Domain:** I register it on my Cloudflare account (agreed with @LNPANDY). Criteria: a neutral name without third-party marks (no "apple", "nintendo", "switch" in it, since a domain is far easier to take away through a trademark complaint than a repository name), auto-renewal on, WHOIS privacy (Cloudflare's default).
2. **Download host:** an R2 bucket on the same account, served at `downloads.<domain>` (a custom domain, because the free `*.r2.dev` address is rate-limited and meant for development). R2 has no egress fees. Only the release workflow and the nightly experimental job write to it, with an API token stored as a repository secret. Files are immutable per version, so nothing can drift from GitHub, and every file is checked against the SHA-256 in the signed manifest anyway.
3. **Landing page:** a static page at `<domain>` (Cloudflare Pages from a folder in this repository, so it deploys on push): what the project is, a download button for the latest release, a short guide (build on the Mac, install on the iPhone or iPad), and links to the README, issues and releases. English and Chinese, matching the launcher. No game names in marketing, no screenshots of games, no donations or ads.
4. **Launcher:** `downloads.<domain>` becomes the second entry in the source list of #267 once the bucket and the workflow step exist and are verified.

**Tasks**
- [ ] Pick and register the domain (me)
- [ ] R2 bucket, custom domain `downloads.<domain>`, API token as repository secret (me)
- [ ] Release workflow and nightly experimental job upload to R2 next to the GitHub release (#227 side)
- [ ] Static page in the repository, deployed with Cloudflare Pages
- [ ] Add the source to the launcher's list (#267 side, @LNPANDY)
- [ ] Link the page from the README

### Outcome

One address that a player can open and download from, a second download source the project controls, and no change to where the project lives: GitHub stays the home for code, issues and pull requests.
title: Project domain, static landing page and a Cloudflare R2 download host

### This is

An idea

### What happens, or what you would like

After an install, `installBuiltApp` asks whether to copy the game data to the device, because a large game's image is many GB over USB. The question is the same every time and knows nothing about the device:

- Rebuilding after a code or shader change asks again, although the game data did not change. Saying yes re-sends several GB; saying no leaves the two sides out of step with no record of it.
- After a game update the prompt looks identical, so skipping it leaves the device running the previous version's data. Nothing says so.

**What would help:** remember, per game and device, which game-data version was last copied there, and use that in the prompt.

- Store it on the library entry next to `installedDevice` (one short identity string, the `romfs.id` the build already writes: `build`, `version`, `size`, index hash — `dm/host/romfs_identity.h`).
- On the next install of the same device, compare the entry's identity with this build's `romfs.id` and say which case it is: "the device already has this version's game data" (offer to skip, default skip), or "the game data changed since the last copy" (ask as it does today, default copy).
- Write the identity only after a successful copy, so an interrupted transfer is asked again.

This needs no new device paths and no change to `devicectl` usage: the copy is the one `installBuiltApp` already performs from `games/<id>`.

**Not in scope:** installing the app and the data separately, uploading from the build folder, or changing how the app finds its data (per-game folder first, then `Documents/romfs.img`, then the bundle — `main.m`).

### Background

This is the useful half of the closed #213, which went further (a `--romfs separate` build, identity checks against a new device path, and uploads driven by the comparison). The discussion there lists what that larger version would have had to get right.

# Cheats do not work on iOS: every entry is turned off with `mprotect … errno 13`

## What happens

v0.7.2 carries the Atmosphère cheat engine. On an iPhone the engine loads and parses the file correctly — right build ID, right entry names — but **every cheat is disabled at startup**:

```
[dm] cheats: writable alias of main not mapped (mprotect toggle fallback)
[dm] cheats: …/Documents/games/0100F2C0115B6000/cheats/277178B7DBA1B6D4.txt: build 277178B7DBA1B6D4
[dm] [RED] cheats: no writable alias of main, code pages go through an mprotect toggle that races with the game's own execution
[dm] [RED] cheat "№ 1. Inf. Health": mprotect of a code page failed (errno 13), turning it off
[dm] [RED] cheat "№ 2. Inf. Stamina": mprotect of a code page failed (errno 13), turning it off
[dm] [RED] cheat "№ 4. Inf. Battery": mprotect of a code page failed (errno 13), turning it off
```

Nothing in the launcher says the file was accepted but the writes were refused, so from the UI it looks like cheats "are on".

Reproduced with TotK 1.4.3 (`0100F2C0115B6000`, build `277178B7DBA1B6D4`, 89 entries, `Documents/games/<TID>/cheats/<BID>.txt` + `.enabled`), slim IPA (`DM_COPY_ROMFS=NO`), iPhone on iOS 27.2.

## Three signing configurations, all fail

| Signing | `get-task-allow` | Debugger | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Third-party distribution profile | `false` | – | 3 × `errno 13` |
| Personal team dev cert | `true` | – | 3 × `errno 13` |
| Same dev cert, launched from Xcode (⌘R) | `true` | yes (`debugserver` present on device) | 3 × `errno 13` |

## Why

`dm/host/hle_cheats.c` compiles the writable-alias path out on iOS:

```c
#if TARGET_OS_IPHONE
static void alias_setup(void) { g_alias = NULL; }   /* mach_vm.h is forbidden by the iOS SDK */
#else
… mach_vm_remap + mach_vm_protect → g_alias
#endif
```

so the only remaining route is the per-page `mprotect` toggle in `main_write_pages`. But the game image is not anonymous memory: `dm/ios/tools/gen_embed.py` puts it in `__TEXT,__dm<name>x0` / `__TEXT,__dm<name>x1` and `loader.c` remaps those pieces into one contiguous range, so the pages keep their code-signing provenance. `mprotect(PROT_WRITE)` on them returns `EACCES`; only an Apple-granted `dynamic-codesigning` entitlement would allow it. `get-task-allow` and a debugger are not enough (measured above, row 3).

Upstream's own PR says the same thing: *"The iPhone: the engine compiles into the iOS host but was not run there; the menu and panel are Mac-only."*

## Related

I filed the technical report upstream: **seedds/nxnative#724** — with the signing matrix, the `alias_setup` stub, and two suggestions (build-time baking of the enabled entries into `patched_*/main.patched.bin`, which needs no entitlement, or mapping the image from anonymous memory, which does).

## What would help users of this fork

1. **Say so in the UI.** When the log contains `mprotect of a code page failed`, the iOS shell could show "cheats are not supported on this platform yet" instead of silently leaving them "on". Right now the only way to find out is to pull `Documents/log.txt`.
2. **Documentation.** The Cheats section of `docs/frontends.md` only describes the folder/env switch, which reads as "set `DM_CHEATS` and it works"; a note that the write path is unimplemented on iPhone would stop this being rediscovered by every user.
3. If build-time baking ever lands upstream, exposing it as a build option here would give iOS users a working path.

Happy to attach the full `log.txt` from all three runs, the generated `xcode/Gen/embed.S`, and `codesign -d --entitlements` output for each build if useful.

body:
Hi, I encountered two issues when using **Manage → Saves** and wanted to ask whether these workflows could be improved.

The game was built with NX2Apple but installed on the phone through another method—for example, signing and installing the exported IPA with LCSign. Although the game runs normally and the Mac can read its application data container, the Saves window still says that the game was not installed from this launcher and disables save transfers.

Also, when both an iPhone and an iPad are paired, querying a device whose connection is not ready can take a long time without returning. Refresh remains available during this time, so repeated clicks can leave the window stuck at “Reading…”.

Would it be possible to:

- **Separate save access from installation and signing records:** discover the corresponding game actually installed on a device without requiring the local Xcode project or cached signed application to remain available.
- Offer an **iPhone/iPad selector** when multiple devices are available, and show which device is currently being queried.
- Add query timeouts and clear error messages, and prevent overlapping refresh requests.
- Support the save layout actually used by the game, such as `Documents/save` or `Documents/games/<title ID>/save`, while retaining the existing confirmation and backup behavior.

We made a temporary fix in a personal fork: [complete patch](https://github.com/Tiomehsh/NX2Apple/blob/f8d5c2979fd46b08ae6cdc5043164b99f65e3433/.personal/save-sync.patch). It has been verified on our own devices, but custom bundle identifiers, unusual save locations, and multiple devices with the same game installed have not been comprehensively covered. The implementation is therefore only a reference, and we are not sure whether it would be suitable to merge directly. We would appreciate your thoughts on the direction.

### Game, title ID and versions

Disney Dreamlight Valley, 0100D39012C1A000, base v0 + update v4259840 (1.25.3), SDK 20.5.21. Provisional profile (no dm/games entry).

### Where it runs

iPhone or iPad (built for iPhone / iPad)

### Device, chip and RAM

iPad Pro 11-inch (3rd generation), iPad13,4, M1, 8 GB

### macOS or iOS / iPadOS version

iPadOS 26.5 (23F77); built on macOS 26.6.2 with Xcode 27.1

### How it was installed

`scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py --platform ios --gpu g13g --romfs separate`, re-signed with an Apple Development profile (entitlement `com.apple.developer.kernel.increased-memory-limit`), installed with `xcrun devicectl device install app`; RomFS pushed with `scripts/push_romfs.sh`.

### NX2Apple version

Branch at `0c10d742` (main at `cdb74c9f` plus a backport of upstream `682fdd26`, two patch areas, which this game's 145.8 MB text needs to build at all). `.upstream-ref` `062cd06e`.

### What happens, and when

The game boots, plays the opening and the character creation, then crashes about halfway through the loading bar after the opening scene, about 2 minutes in. Same place on every attempt.

```
[dm] CRASH sig=11 addr=0 pc=main+0x12a2150 lr=main+0x12a2114
```

**Cause.** At `main+0x12a2110`, Unity grows a table (the object ID map, about 773k objects at that point) and asks its allocator for (0x1fffff + 1) × 32 = 64 MB. The allocator returns NULL, and the store at `main+0x12a2150` writes through it. Memory is not short: the process is at 2.4 GB resident, and the guest has mapped 1.75 GB of a 3.21 GB pool. Address space is short:

- `DM_REGIONS` on the Mac, same save, same route: one caller, `main+0x22e505c`, makes 4,236 address regions, with 3.26 GB reserved for 1.68 GB mapped. They reach the top of the profile's 4.375 GB alias region (+4.375 GB). 1.1 GB is still free, but in gaps of at most 186 MB, so the 64 MB aligned block finds no place.
- The Mac reproduces the crash at the same pc with the profile's alias region.
- With `DM_ALIAS_SIZE=0x1000000000` (64 GB) on the Mac, the same route passes the loading screen and plays in the valley for 10 minutes, with no crash. The regions reach 3.93 GB reserved and 2.04 GB mapped, spread up to +42 GB.
- Not the cause: `DM_PROF_APP_POOL=0xA0000000` (2.5 GB) crashed at the same pc. StandardAllocator is not involved: no cap is logged, and no region of 256 MB or more is made.

**What made it work on the iPad.** Two changes together:

1. Re-signing with `com.apple.developer.kernel.extended-virtual-addressing` added next to `increased-memory-limit`.
2. `DM_ALIAS_SIZE=0x400000000` (16 GB) in `Documents/env.txt`.

With both, the game passes the loading screen and plays normally.

**Question for the profile.** `hle_svc.c` says "an iPhone has no room for more than the profile's" alias region, and the build adds only `increased-memory-limit`. This game needs more than 4.375 GB of alias address space on iOS. Is the extended virtual addressing entitlement acceptable for a game's build, for example as a profile key that adds it and sets a larger `mem_alias`? Sideloaders that drop unknown entitlements would still get the 4.375 GB region and this crash. I can send a profile for the game once the approach is settled.

**Proposed change.** Expose this as a build option. Most of the plumbing exists: `build_ipa.sh` takes `DM_ENTITLEMENTS`, and the host reads `DM_ALIAS_SIZE`, which a build switch could put in the bundle's `dm/env.txt`.

- **Launcher (`frontend/`), on the build page:**
  - An "Extended virtual addressing" entitlement checkbox, next to the existing increased memory limit.
  - A "Game address space" size field, enabled only while that box is ticked. It sets the alias region, not the application pool: changing the pool does not help, as above. Without the entitlement, iOS refuses a single reservation over about 6 GB and the host stops at launch ("reserve guest AS").
- **Default size:** the profile's `mem_alias` when the box is unticked, and 16 GB when it is ticked. 16 GB is tested here; 8 GB would probably do for this game (about 4 GB reserved in total) but is untested. Changing the default for every game would also enlarge StandardAllocator's address space through the gate in `stdalloc_init`, so it should stay opt-in.
- **Profile key:** a key, for example the game needing a larger address space, so the launcher pre-ticks the box for games like this one.
- **Free Apple accounts:** they may not get this entitlement; this needs checking. `Devices.swift` already knows which teams are free, so the box could be disabled for them.
- **Unsigned IPAs:** the entitlement only works if the sideloader keeps it when re-signing. The option could note that.

body:
### Idea

**Connect the Mac launcher and the iPhone/iPad shell over the local network: build status on the phone, game data and installs without a cable.**

Today everything that goes from the Mac to the iPhone needs the cable (`devicectl`) or a sideloading tool, and the phone knows nothing about a build until the app arrives. Once the iOS shell exists (Route C, #144, views in #226), the shell can talk to the Mac launcher directly.

**1. Build status on the phone (Bonjour)**
- The Mac launcher advertises a Bonjour service (e.g. `_nx2apple._tcp`), the shell finds it with `NWBrowser` (Network framework).
- The launcher forwards the NSP script's existing `--progress json` stream: game, stage, percent, done or failed with the failure row's reason.
- iOS asks once for local network access (`NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription`, `NSBonjourServices` in the shell's Info.plist).

**2. Game data without a cable**
- Over the same connection, Mac to phone. With `includePeerToPeer` the Network framework also uses AWDL (what AirDrop uses underneath), so it works without a shared Wi-Fi.
- The "game data once per game and version" logic from #213 carries over: the phone reports which data identity (`romfs.id`) it has, the Mac sends only what is missing or different.
- Large transfers keep running when the app is in the background: the Mac serves the files over HTTPS and the phone downloads them with a background `URLSession`.
- Expect tens of MB/s over Wi-Fi or AWDL (minutes for a large game). The cable stays the fast option.

**3. Installing the app without a cable**
- `devicectl` already installs over Wi-Fi to a device that was paired with the Mac once and is on the same network. The launcher can offer that when no cable is connected. Signing stays on the Mac.

**Security (required, not optional)**
- **Pairing:** the first connection shows a short code on both screens, the player confirms it. Only paired devices are served.
- **Encryption:** every connection is TLS. Network-framework connections use TLS with a pre-shared key from the pairing. The HTTPS server for background downloads uses a self-signed certificate whose fingerprint is exchanged during pairing, and the phone pins it (the background session's trust challenge checks the fingerprint). Each request also carries a per-device token.
- Nothing is reachable without pairing, nothing is announced beyond the service name, and the server runs only while the launcher is open and a transfer or status session is active. Game files never become available to other devices on the network.

**Order**
- [ ] Depends on the shell being wired to the engine (Route C M2 and later). Not worth doing for today's single-game apps.
- [ ] Step 1: Bonjour discovery, pairing, build status
- [ ] Step 2: game data transfer with the #213 identity check, background downloads
- [ ] Step 3: wireless install through `devicectl`

### Outcome

Opening the shell on the iPhone shows the Mac's library and the state of a running build. "Add to iPhone" builds on the Mac, shows progress live on the phone, and sends the game data over the air, encrypted and only to paired devices.
title: Mac launcher and iOS shell over the local network: build status on the phone, game data and installs without a cable

body:
### Idea

**The next step after the patch queue (#123): stop committing the engine, keep only the pin and the patches.**

**Where we are.** Since #124 the engine is fully described by two things: `.upstream-ref` (the seedds/nxnative commit we build on) and `patches/` (what we change on top, with `Upstream-Status`, `Reason` and `Issue` for every patch). `patches.py apply` rebuilds `dm/`, `scripts/`, `docs/`, `ref/` and `AGENTS.md` from them, and `patches.py check` verifies in CI that the committed tree equals pin plus series. So the committed tree is already a derived product. We still check it in, and that costs a lot:
- 2,255 of the repository's 2,467 files (91 %, about 290 MB) are this copy of upstream.
- Every bump rewrites hundreds of vendored files in one PR, and every engine fix shows up twice, as the patch file and as the tree change.
- An engine fix is a commit on a generated tree, then `export` or `absorb` into the right patch. It works, but it is the most error-prone step in the queue (we hit it again today on #162, where `absorb` picked the wrong patch).
- The vendored tree has no upstream history, so `git log` and `git blame` on an engine file show our bumps, not seedds' commits.

**Proposal.** Debian (orig tarball plus `debian/patches`), Electron (Chromium fetched at a pinned revision plus `patches/`), OpenWrt and Yocto all work this way: the repository holds the pin and the patches, and the upstream source is fetched and patched where it is needed.

1. **The repository keeps** the launcher (`frontend/`, `frontend-qt/`), `.upstream-ref`, `patches/` and the patch tooling, moved from `scripts/patches.py` (a vendored path) to `tools/`.
2. **`dm/`, `scripts/`, `docs/`, `ref/` and `AGENTS.md` leave git** and go into `.gitignore`.
3. **`tools/engine.py sync`** fetches seedds/nxnative at the pin (a shallow fetch of that one commit) into `engine/`, a real git repository, and applies the series there with `git am`, one commit per patch. It writes a stamp of pin plus series, so it only runs again when one of them changed.
4. **Working on the engine** happens in `engine/`: a fix is a commit there, `git format-patch` turns it into a patch with the header, and the same commit can go upstream as a pull request directly from that tree. `git log` and `git blame` show seedds' real history.
5. **The launcher** runs `engine.py sync` after an update when the stamp changed, and calls `engine/scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py`. The Qt front end does the same.
6. **The release app** (`build-mac-app.yml`) embeds the synced `engine/`, so a player who installs a release needs no extra download on the first start.
7. **CI** runs `engine.py sync` as its first step. `patches.py check` is no longer needed, since there is no committed tree that can drift. Reviews of an engine patch get the applied diff as a CI comment, so a reviewer still sees the change in place.
8. **The nightly bump** stays as it is: move the pin, apply the series, drop patches upstream has, open a PR. The PR then only touches `.upstream-ref` and `patches/`.

**What it costs**
- A one-time migration: the launcher's paths in Swift and Qt, the workflows that read `dm/` or `scripts/` (`tests.yml`, `pr-scope.yml`, `sync-upstream.yml`, `daily-health.yml`, `issue-triage.yml`), the issue forms, and links from our README into `dm/`, which then point to seedds at the pin.
- A source checkout needs one `engine.py sync` (and network access to github.com/seedds) before the first build. Release apps do not, since they carry the engine.
- GitHub's code search in this repository no longer finds engine code. seedds' repository has it.

**Working with AI agents.** Agents read the engine the same way they read it today, from files on disk. Three things make sure they find it:
- `engine/` is in `.gitignore`, since it is a build product like `.build/`. Claude Code's search is based on ripgrep and skips ignored paths, so a root `.ignore` file with `!/engine/` makes the folder searchable again while git keeps ignoring it. The draft PR tests that a search from the repository root finds engine files.
- A SessionStart hook in `.claude/settings.json` runs `tools/engine.py sync` when the stamp is stale, so a session never starts without the engine or on an old pin.
- `CLAUDE.md` points to `engine/AGENTS.md` instead of `AGENTS.md`. Upstream's agent guides (`docs/agents/`, the symptom index, the game notes) stay where upstream keeps them, in `engine/docs/` and `engine/dm/games/`, and are always current.

A patch from an agent is then a commit in `engine/` plus `tools/engine.py export`, and the upstream pull request goes from the same commit. Agent briefs change from "edit `dm/`, then `patches.py export`" to "work in `engine/`, then `tools/engine.py export`".

**What stays the same.** The patch policy from #123: upstream first, `forwarded` while a fix is in review there, `fork-only` only with a reason, and no patches to the shader chain or the tool pins. Patches we must carry are carried exactly as today.

**Plan**
- [ ] Agree on the direction here (@LNPANDY, this is your call)
- [ ] Draft PR: `tools/engine.py`, the launcher's paths, CI and the release workflow, after the PRs that are open now have merged (they edit the same launcher files)
- [ ] One release with both layouts working, then remove the committed tree
- [ ] With the committed tree gone, the repository gets **its own `AGENTS.md`** for the fork. Upstream's `AGENTS.md` describes seedds/nxnative and stays in `engine/` for engine work. Ours covers what is NX2Apple's: the layout (launchers, `tools/`, `engine/`, `patches/`), commit with your own git identity and never upstream's (upstream's file ends with a `git -c user.name=seedds` line written for its own repository), upstream first for engine and game profile changes (a seedds/nxnative PR plus a `forwarded` patch, `fork-only` only with a reason), how to turn a commit in `engine/` into a patch and the same commit into an upstream PR, and the rules for issues and PRs (templates, labels, people as @login). `CLAUDE.md` then points to it and keeps only what is specific to Claude.

### Outcome

A repository that holds only what is ours: the launcher, the pin and a short list of patches with their reasons. Engine work happens in a real nxnative checkout with its history, and fixes go upstream from the same tree.
title: Engine: keep only the pin and the patches, fetch and patch seedds/nxnative where it is needed

### What happens, and when

Two rendering defects, in every scene I tried, at any time of day, every time. Both are identical on update 2.1.0 and 3.0.1.

**A. Hard-edged dark box in the lighting** (mostly indoors / under decks, e.g. Pont de récupération). A region with perfectly sharp edges is much darker than the rest of the scene. It is not in the original game.
- Same spot, same camera, three times of day (05:5x, 08:0x, 10:4x): the region has the same shape each time, and its darkness grows with the time of day (faint at dawn, near black at 08:0x and 10:4x while the lit side outside is bright).
- The edges look like a world-space box seen in perspective: a vertical edge, a diagonal edge where it meets the floor, a horizontal top edge with a step.
- It also shows as a lighter translucent rectangle in other places (Bazar d'Argentum).

**B. Stretched geometry streaks.** Long thin wedges or streaks from small objects and characters: a brown wedge next to the NPC "Bonbon" (Bazar d'Argentum), a long dotted streak across a staircase, a horizontal line cutting an NPC at sunset, characters stretching. They remain when the lighting pass is replaced by solid magenta (below), so they do not come from that pass.

**What I found**
- `DM_NVN_HILITE=93d0e7a7c14cdfb0` (solid magenta): the whole screen turns magenta, the dark box disappears, the streaks stay. That pixel shader is `/bf2.ard/monolib/shader/shd_lgt.wishp ... HCPS ... var4.3` (pair with VS `468bd9c28161136f`), the indirect-lighting pass. Caveat: a solid colour hides everything, so this only shows the box is produced by, or hidden by, that pass.
- That shader samples 4 2D textures, one cube-map array (slot 5) and 3 uniform buffers (c5, c6 and one more).
- Weak lead, may be benign: in a `DM_NVN_TEXINFO=64x64` run, 3 of the 21 64x64 cube-map arrays (serials 3379, 3386, 3393) had far fewer non-zero bytes (2-4 KB against 20-32 KB for the others).
- Log: one `[RED] texture type mismatch` (startup shader `da21866ffe3a9d7a`), which the game README says is unrelated. `shader keys not in the shader map (another game version): 4`.
- The queue raster-origin fix (merged 2026-10-28) is in this build.

**Tried, no visible change on A or B**

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Update 2.1.0 vs 3.0.1 | same on both |
| `DM_NVN_LAZY_CLEAR=0` | no change |
| `DM_NVN_CUT=0` | no change |
| `DM_NVN_TBDR=1` | no change |
| `DM_NVN_FB_SNAP=all` | no change on A or B. Only two shaders sample their own pass (`83eefd80f5194c07` 128x128 and `b1f6c2a6c67bd636`, shd_cloud.wishp); the clouds disappear with it |
| `DM_NVN_DISPATCH_OWN=1` | no change |
| `DM_NVN_CLEARLOG=1` | no log line over about 9900 frames, including the dark-box scene |
| 64x64x32 3D textures | not used by the lighting shader |

**Suspicions (not verified)**
- A: the cube-map array lookup of the indirect-lighting shader (array layer or face addressing for the probe covering that volume), or the uniform data that selects the probe.
- B: vertex inputs. 256 vertex shaders use gl_VertexIndex together with a dynamic uniform-array access and a cb_extent.tsv entry (e.g. `00717317b42d5543` slot 1:528 B, `01da68e1cc9d8e5c` slot 1:560 B). If an extent is too small for a draw with many vertices, the later vertices would read zeros. I have not tested this.

The original game look: no dark box, no stretched streaks.

title: Xenoblade Chronicles 2 (0100E95004038000): hard-edged dark box in the lighting and stretched geometry streaks on Mac (Apple M5)

body:
### Which step failed

Prepare Xcode, app build or IPA pack

### The message

The build succeeds, but selected DLC is missing from both the slim IPA and the exported game-data folder. Existing DLC-dependent saves cannot load.

Reproduction:
1. Select base game 1.0.0, update 1.0.1 and DLC 0100B8A026F15002 in the GUI.
2. Build for iPhone/iPad using the default slim IPA workflow.
3. DLC extraction succeeds and <work>/aoc/2.img exists.
4. The IPA contains no Payload/DmIOS.app/aoc/, and games/0100B8A026F14000/ contains only romfs.img.
5. An existing save requiring the DLC cannot load.

Verified workaround: add the already-extracted 2.img to Payload/DmIOS.app/aoc/2.img, re-sign and reinstall while retaining the save and external game data. The same old save then loads successfully (confirmed on device).

Code-path findings in the affected checkout:

body:
Version **0.6.0** (`6fd0f95`), iPhone 17 (A19, 5-core G18P, 8 GB), iOS 27.2.

**Symptom.** I built *The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom* (`01008CF01BAAC000`, v196608) for the iPhone. The settings page shows, under Performance, **Metal 4 pipelines off** and **Pipeline prebuild on**. A player reads that as "the prebuild is doing its work" and moves on. It is not: with Metal 4 pipelines off there is no archive for the prebuild to fill, and both of its entry points return before doing anything. Every new pipeline is still compiled while the game waits — the stutter the prebuild exists to remove.

Nothing on the page says the two are related, and the player has nowhere to fix it: the pairing comes from the defaults the packer writes, so the only way out is to discover, by other means, that switching the *first* toggle on is what makes the second one mean something.

**Root cause.**

1. `dm/games/settings.tsv:31` — `DM_PSO_PREBUILD` carries a hard-coded default `1` and an empty meta column, so it is drawn whenever `gfxapi:nvn` holds, with no `needs=`. The same table already does this correctly one row group up: `:27` (`DM_RUMBLE_GAIN`) ends in `needs=DM_RUMBLE=1`.
2. `dm/games/settings.tsv:30` — `DM_PSO_MTL4` defaults to `DM_GAME_PSO_MTL4|1`. `dm/games/settings.py:81-86` splits that on `|` into iOS|Mac and, on iOS, resolves it through the profile header's `DM_GAME_PSO_MTL4`. A game whose profile has no `pso_mtl4 on` gets `0` there, while `1` is taken on the Mac. This is why the contradiction is iOS-only: on the Mac the same table yields `Metal 4 pipelines on`, and the prebuild works.
3. `dm/gfx/nvn/nvn_mtl.m:6229` — `prepare_prebuild()` opens with `if (!hybrid_on()) return;`. With Metal 4 pipelines off, the prebuild does not run and prints nothing, so nothing in the log contradicts the page.
4. `dm/gfx/nvn/nvn_mtl.m:5946` — the background path, `pso_prebuild_bg()`, guards the same way (`if (!hybrid_on() || prepare_on()) return;`). There is no third path: `mtl_pso_prebuild_tool()` (`:5934`) only answers `DM_PSO_PREBUILD=tool`, which is the build-time tool, not the app.
5. `dm/games/settings.py:100-104` — `needs` is parsed and validated (the named variable must exist and must be able to take that value) but never required, so a table row may depend on something and simply not say so.

**One reproducible check.** Read the settings list the packer wrote for this game:

```bash
python3 -c "import json; d=json.load(open('DmIOS.app/dm/launcher.json')); \
print([(r['label'], r['default']) for r in d['settings'] if 'pipeline' in r['label'].lower()])"
# [('Metal 4 pipelines', '0'), ('Pipeline prebuild', '1')]
```

Then start the game and look at the line `nvn_mtl.m:5207` writes:

```
render pipelines through the MTLDevice (iOS: DM_PSO_MTL4=1 or the profile key pso_mtl4 on turns on the Metal 4 bases, the pipeline archive and the hybrid pipelines)
```

That line says the run has no archive at all, while the page the player just dismissed said the prebuild was on.

**What works today** (verified on this build): switch **Metal 4 pipelines** on. The prebuild then appears to mean what it says — the first start waits once behind "Preparing pipelines", and every start after it skips the step. For any game whose profile does not set `pso_mtl4 on`, that manual toggle is currently the only way to get a prebuild at all.

**Suggestions, in the order I would do them**

1. **`settings.tsv:31`: append `needs=DM_PSO_MTL4=1`.** One line, the same form `:27` already uses, and `settings.py:100-104` will accept it as it stands (`DM_PSO_MTL4` is a toggle, so its value set is `{0, 1}`). The row then appears only once Metal 4 pipelines is on — which is also where the player first needs to see it, since turning that toggle on is what makes the prebuild appear, defaulted to `1`. The page can no longer advertise a prebuild that is not running.
2. **`docs/settings.md:140`: say when the row exists.** The paragraph ends with "It needs Metal 4 pipelines." — accurate, but the reader is left to connect it to the row above. One clause about the row appearing only while that option is on would close the loop, the way the "Hold frames when late" section already explains its own condition (`Frame rate` only).
3. Not needed, mentioned for completeness: `settings.py` could also rewrite the default of a row whose `needs` is unmet. With 1 in place there is nothing left for it to fix, and a static table stays easier to read.

Not urgent for me — nothing crashes, and anyone who turns Metal 4 pipelines on gets exactly what the page promised. It is worth a line of the table, though, because the default lands every iOS player of every game without `pso_mtl4 on` in a state where the settings page describes a step that is not happening, and a player has no reason to doubt it.
title: iOS settings offer "Pipeline prebuild: on" for games whose Metal 4 pipelines default to off, where the prebuild never runs

Five UX gaps found during the owner's new-user test of the onboarding flow (v0.6.0, fresh macOS user account). All are about telling the user what to do next, not about functionality.

### 1. Background dependency install shows "failed" before "done"

The `.NET` row in the onboarding's background-install list briefly showed the failure state, then flipped to success a few seconds later. The row needs an explicit **"installing…"** state between the button press and the outcome — the spinner exists in the dependency panel but the onboarding's own list does not use it.

### 2. The Xcode step does not say "open the App Store" clearly enough

A new user who has never opened Xcode sees the Xcode step but the guidance to go to the App Store is not prominent. The step should say, in large text: **"Xcode is not installed — open the App Store to download it (free)"** with a button that opens `macappstore://apps.apple.com/app/id497799835`.

Note: on a multi-user Mac where another account already has Xcode installed, the new user's `xcode-select -p` still points at CommandLineTools, and `/Applications/Xcode.app` exists. The detection should recognise this state and say "Xcode is already installed on this Mac — just open it once" instead of "Xcode is not installed".

### 3. Does a fresh Xcode include the iOS SDK?

**No.** Since Xcode 15, the iOS SDK ships as a separate download (`xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS`). A fresh App Store install has `xcodebuild` but no iOS SDK. The first launch of Xcode prompts to install additional components (which includes the iOS SDK), or the app's own flow downloads it. This should be stated in the onboarding so the user knows what to expect.

### 4. The Xcode dependency row should say "you do not need the iOS Simulator"

Xcode's Components page auto-downloads the iOS Simulator runtime (~8 GB) alongside the iOS SDK. The app never uses the simulator. When the Xcode row shows the SDK is ready (or after the first launch), add a note: "You do not need the iOS Simulator (~8 GB) — cancel it if Xcode offers to download one."

### 5. The signing guidance needs English menu paths and more detail

When no Apple ID certificate exists, the guidance text (in the Install group) tells the user to sign in to Xcode but uses Chinese menu names. Xcode itself has no Chinese localization, so the user cannot find the menu. The guidance should say, in both languages:

> Open **Xcode → Settings → Apple Accounts** (the menu is in English), sign in with your Apple ID, select **Personal Team**, then click **Download Manual Profiles**. Wait ~30 seconds for the certificate to appear, then press Check again.

Also: the certificate does not appear immediately after sign-in — the user had to download it manually (Manage Certificates → +) and wait before the app detected it. The guidance should mention this delay.
title: Onboarding and dependency UX: five gaps from the owner's new-user test

Games that support local wireless play (Pokémon trades and battles, Mario Kart, Smash, …) should be playable with friends over the internet, the way Ryujinx's LDN did, without any server run by the project. The owner agreed to the idea.

**Shape**
- The host implements the `ldn` service, and the game uses its normal local mode.
- One player opens a room in the launcher, which starts a small relay on their own Mac. Friends join with a room code, from the Mac or the iPhone app. No accounts, no central server, nothing stored. Anyone can also run the relay on their own server.
- The launcher explains reachability simply: UPnP, port forwarding, or a tool like Tailscale.

**Where it lives**
- Ask seedds whether he wants `ldn` in nxnative. If yes, it lands upstream.
- If not, it goes in this fork as a fork-only patch: almost entirely new files (`dm/host/hle_ldn.c`, picked up by the Makefile's `hle_*.c`), plus one service-registration hook, which we'd still offer upstream on its own.
- The relay and the launcher UI are fork code either way.

**Out of scope:** Nintendo's servers, console certificates, accounts, friend lists.

**Wording:** "local wireless play over the internet". No promotion of specific games' online features.

**Steps**
- [ ] Ask seedds about `ldn` in the host (after his current review queue)
- [ ] `ldn` service in the host (upstream or fork patch)
- [ ] Relay (open source, self-hostable)
- [ ] Launcher: open / join a room (view layer first, then wiring)
- [ ] iOS: local network permission, join from the iPhone app
title: Local wireless play over the internet (LDN), self-hosted

body:
Two gaps in the iPhone install flow, both from the same cause: the tool installs through `xcodebuild` + `devicectl` and never writes an `.ipa`.

## 1. A deleted app can only come back by rebuilding

After "Install on the iPhone" there is no package file, only the signed `DmIOS.app` inside `<id>_build/xcode-derived-data/Build/Products/Release-iphoneos/`. If the user deletes the app on the device, the only way back is to run the whole build again (or find that folder by hand).

**What it should do**

- Keep the signed `.app` (already there) and offer **Reinstall** on the finished-install card: `devicectl device install app` on the existing bundle, no re-extract, no re-sign — seconds.
- Offer **Save IPA…** as well, so a user can keep an installable package (the signed app + a Payload/ zip), for a Mac that will be away from the phone.

## 2. A free Apple ID's 7-day signature cannot be renewed

An app installed this way is signed with a development profile that expires after 7 days; sideloaders (AltStore/Sideloadly) renew *their own* installs, not ours. Today the only renewal is a full rebuild.

**What it should do**

- A **Renew** button on the installed game (and on the library row): re-run `xcodebuild -allowProvisioningUpdates` with the cached project and derived data (the app is already built — this is a re-sign, not a rebuild), then `devicectl device install`. The Documents container is preserved because the bundle ID does not change.
- Show the profile's expiry date next to the device (read it from the embedded.mobileprovision) and warn a day before.
- If the provisioning profile cannot be refreshed while offline or the certificate was revoked, say so and name the fix (sign in to Xcode → Accounts → Manage Certificates).

## Notes

- Both are launcher-frontend work over existing pieces: `installBuiltApp` already has the devicectl call; the signed bundle is already on disk; `-allowProvisioningUpdates` is already how signing works.
- The renewal must not touch game data: the game folder stays in `Documents/games/<id>/`, and the same bundle ID keeps the container.
- A free account can only renew while its certificate is valid; after expiry the *renewal* itself needs Xcode to create a new certificate, which `-allowProvisioningUpdates` does when signed in.
title: iPhone install: reinstall from the cached signed app, and renew a free Apple ID's 7-day signature

body:
Every failure a user can hit should tell them what to type or click next. Today two reports cost a diagnosis round-trip each because the message stopped at the symptom:

- a broken Homebrew (`/opt/homebrew is not writable`) makes the five dependency rows fail in under a second, with the brew output only in the log the user never opened — see the diagnostics in the dependency-install report;
- a `romfs.img` build on 0.5.0 died at the shader split with `zstd ... returned non-zero exit status 1` without saying "this image contains files zstd cannot open by path — update the repository" (issue #118).

## What to do

Walk every user-facing failure path and make the message self-solving: what failed, why in one sentence, and the exact command/button to fix it. Cover at least:

1. **Dependencies**: brew missing / brew present but not writable / a package install fails (show the brew error line inline, under the row, not only in the log); Python too old vs missing vs venv creation failed; .NET missing.
2. **Keys**: prod.keys missing or unreadable; a container the check cannot read (state that the build proceeds).
3. **Game files**: damaged NSP (re-dump or `--allow-damaged`); a folder with several games; a stale `.nx2apple-library`; game data on an unmounted drive.
4. **Build steps**: Rosetta Python, missing iOS SDK, missing glslangValidator/Metal toolchain, disk space, Xcode signing (team taken → team variant retry; no certificate → sign in to Xcode), devicectl transfer failed.
5. **Runtime**: the launcher's "no game data" state (already improved), a re-signed build's stale bookmark (already improved).

Each row gets the message text in en + zh, a test that the string contains the actionable part (the command or the button name), and — where the app can do it itself — a button next to the message instead of a sentence ("Fix ownership…", "Open Xcode accounts", "Update repository").

The pattern to copy is the keys row: it names the missing key and the firmware generation, and never shows key values.

Closing note for whoever takes it: this replaces the bundled-tools direction for now (PR #121 was declined on its macOS floor), so the messages are the only path a Homebrew-less user has.
title: Every failure message should tell the user what to do next (dependencies first)

body:
**Summary**

When a game's files are selected from more than one folder, the GUI stages them into a fresh temporary directory (`nsport-<UUID>`) on every build and deletes it afterwards. The provisional profile lives under that staging dir, and the profile files are part of the input fingerprints of `split_shaders()` and `build_shaders()` in `scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py`. Because the staging path changes every build, those fingerprints never match on the next run — so shader split and the iOS/Mac shader build recompute from scratch even when their previous products are complete on disk.

Users who keep all files in a single folder never hit this: the profile path is stable there.

**Impact**

On a large title (73,496 shaders), the iOS shader step alone took ~3.5 hours on the previous run. Any rebuild — e.g. after a signing failure caused by a locked phone — pays the full cost again.

**Evidence**

Recomputing the fingerprints with the script's own functions, against a completed build:

- `rewrite()` fingerprint matches the stored key (correctly reused).
- `split_shaders()` fingerprint does **not** match its stored key (stored `28a280e2…`, recomputed `d68e86ae…`), even though a complete product is present: `shader/pkg` with 8 files and a note of 73,496 shaders. On rerun, split started over (a fresh `shader/pkg.partial` appeared; the previous split log was empty).

The reuse check in `split_shaders()` only asks "did the input fingerprint change?" and never "are the products still there?".

**Suggested direction**

Verify the products themselves (existence, file count/size, spot hashes) in addition to input fingerprints, and/or keep the profile under the work dir instead of the per-build staging dir. A PR implementing the product-verification approach follows.

**Environment**

NX2Apple v0.5.0 (30559cf), macOS arm64.
title: Shader split and iOS shader steps always recompute when game files span multiple folders

title: Upstream sync failed at 062cd06

body:
### This is
An idea

### What happens, or what you would like
**The problem.** The nightly upstream sync breaks again and again (#92, #104, #105). The cause is in how the fork follows seedds/nxnative. The fork has no shared git history with upstream, so `scripts/sync_upstream.py` takes upstream's files and re-applies the fork's changes by text anchors: 14 patch functions, 97 OURS entries, about 2,300 lines. seedds lands dozens of commits a day, and whenever one of them touches a line near an anchor, the sync stops on main. Fork edits that have no patcher are overwritten silently: `dm/mac/launcher.c`, the runtime-profile edits in `hle_svc.c`, and others.

**What we actually need:**
- fix things in the engine **quickly and on our own**, without waiting for upstream;
- know for every change we carry **why we carry it and where it stands upstream**;
- send fixes **back upstream**, and drop them **automatically** once upstream has them;
- have a new upstream version that conflicts with one of our changes **fail as a reviewable PR**, not as a broken main.

Linux distributions solved exactly this a long time ago. Debian keeps pristine upstream source plus `debian/patches/` (quilt, with DEP-3 headers such as `Forwarded:` and `Applied-Upstream:`). Fedora lists `Patch:` lines in the spec. Electron carries its Chromium changes as `patches/` with a `.patches` series file, applies them with `git am -3`, and exports them back with a script.

**Proposal: a patch queue on top of a pinned upstream**
1. **Pinned, pristine upstream.** `.upstream-ref` stays the pin. The vendored tree is generated, not hand-edited: upstream at the pin, plus our patches.
2. **`patches/`, one patch per change.**
   - Each patch is a `git format-patch` file in a series file that sets the order.
   - Each one carries a short header:

     ```
     Upstream-Status: forwarded seedds/nxnative#475 | pending | fork-only | backport <commit>
     Reason: <one line>
     Issue: LNPANDY/NX2Apple#<n>
     ```

   - Fork-only additions such as new files are patches too, so OURS goes away.
3. **Applying uses a real 3-way merge.** `git am -3` onto the pinned upstream tolerates nearby upstream edits that break today's text anchors.
4. **Bumping upstream** is a script plus the nightly job:
   1. Move the pin.
   2. Re-apply the series.
   3. Drop patches that now apply empty, because upstream has them (`--empty=drop`), and list them as "landed upstream".
   4. Run CI.
   5. Open a **PR** with the result, never a direct push to main.

   When a patch conflicts, the PR carries the conflict and names the patch, its reason and its upstream status. Whoever owns that patch refreshes it.
5. **A quick fix** is an ordinary commit on the generated tree. `scripts/patches.py export` turns it into a new patch with the header. The same change goes upstream as a PR and is marked `forwarded`. Once upstream merges it, the next bump drops it.
6. **Visibility.** `scripts/patches.py status` lists every patch, its upstream status and its age. That gives a short "what we carry and why" list, and the list should keep shrinking.

**Migration.** The current fork changes become the first series, one patch per logical change: runtime profile, per-game data folders, slim IPA, BC on the CPU, key map, `--work-dir`, and so on. Several of them are already in review upstream (#475, #386, #460, #486), and a few are obsolete (the 3.9 notes, the save-load freeze fix, the ROMFSARC layer, `hle_time.c`). `sync_upstream.py`'s anchor patchers and OURS are then retired.

**Longer term.** Once the series is small, the engine can stay unmodified upstream at a pinned commit, and NX2Apple can be the launcher plus a short patch list.

### What you expected
A sync that keeps main green: upstream changes arrive as PRs, conflicts are visible per patch, our own fixes can land the same day, and fixes that upstream takes disappear from our list on their own.

Not applicable: repository tooling.

body:
### Which step failed

Something else

### The message

The rewrite stage of a **derived profile** (a base version the game's profile does not register) fails with `KeyError: 6` in `dm/tools/nso_syms.py:29 dynsyms()`, and with `KeyError: 2` in `dm/tools/patch_nso.py:465 rd()` once the first one is patched locally.

The game's modules are from a 2017 build (NintendoSDK 3): their NSOs use **32-bit ELF structures**, while both readers assume the 64-bit layouts.

### Cause 1 — `nso_syms.dynsyms`

- dynamic table: 8-byte entries (`u32 tag`, `u32 value`) instead of `Elf64_Dyn`'s 16-byte entries. Read as 16-byte entries, `MOD0.dynamic` gives a garbage tag set with no `DT_SYMTAB`, so `tags[6]` raises `KeyError: 6`.
- symbol table: 16-byte entries (`Elf32_Sym`: name, value, size, info, other, shndx) instead of 24-byte `Elf64_Sym`. The tables agree: for this `main`, `DT_STRTAB - DT_SYMTAB = 0x3690 = 873 x 16`, and `DT_HASH`'s chain count is 873.

Verified against the extraction on disk:

```python
for i in range(4096):
    t, v = struct.unpack_from('<II', img, dyn + i * 8)
    if t == 0: break
    tags.setdefault(t, v)
# -> {3: 0xccc18c, 2: 0x16b8, 23: 0xb3c838, 20: 0x11, 17: 0xa5c040, 18: 0xe07f8, ...,
#     6: 0xb3f5a8, 5: 0xb42c38, 4: 0xb3def0, 1: 0x9ac4, 12: 0x24, 13: 0x210, ...}
```

With that fallback, `dynsyms` returns 872 symbols for `main` (`deflateInit2_`, `deflateEnd`, `_ZN2nn6socket13GetHostByNameEPKc`, ...), 14,932 for `sdk`, 1,746 for `subsdk0`; a modern (SDK 9.3.1) `main` I had on hand still parses to 544 symbols, so a fallback keyed on `5 not in tags or 6 not in tags` does not regress the 64-bit path.

```diff
     tags = {}
     for i in range(4096):
         t, v = struct.unpack_from('<qQ', img, dyn + i * 16)
         if t == 0: break
         tags.setdefault(t, v)
+    if 5 not in tags or 6 not in tags:   # SDK 3 and older: 32-bit structures (8-byte Dyn, 16-byte Sym)
+        tags = {}
+        for i in range(4096):
+            t, v = struct.unpack_from('<II', img, dyn + i * 8)
+            if t == 0: break
+            tags.setdefault(t, v)
+        if 5 not in tags or 6 not in tags: raise KeyError(f'no dynamic symbols (MOD0 at {mod0:#x})')
+        symtab, strtab = tags[6], tags[5]
+        n = struct.unpack_from('<I', img, tags[4] + 4)[0] if 4 in tags else (strtab - symtab) // 16
+        out = []
+        for i in range(1, n):
+            name, value, size, info, other, shndx = struct.unpack_from('<IIIBBH', img, symtab + i * 16)
+            s = img[strtab + name:img.index(b'\0', strtab + name)].decode('latin1')
+            if s: out.append((s, shndx != 0, info >> 4))
+        return out
     symtab, strtab = tags[6], tags[5]
```

### Cause 2 — `patch_nso.rd`

The same era problem in the rewriter: the DWARF `eh_frame_hdr` encoding table is `{0x3, 0xB, 0x4}` only, and this module's FDE count is encoded as `DW_EH_PE_udata2` (format 2). `0x1` (udata1), `0x2` (udata2), `0x5` (sdata4) and `0xD` (sdata2) are missing.

I did not patch this one: I cannot verify the rest of the rewriter (spin-wait rules, SDK patches) for a build nobody has brought up.

### What I would expect

A base version an old profile does not register should either build from its derived profile, or stop with one line naming the version and the reason, instead of a Python traceback. # Mac apps are always built in English: no language choice in the GUI, and the Mac launcher cannot change it afterwards

Version **0.5.0** (`30559cf`), macOS 27.0.1.

**Symptom.** I built *The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom* (`01008CF01BAAC000`, v196608) as a Mac app from the GUI. It runs, but its UI is English. The game has no in-game language menu — like most Nintendo titles it takes the console's language — and its `control.nacp` lists 15 languages, `zh-Hans` and `zh-Hant` among them. So a player has no way to get Chinese in either place they would look: not at build time, not in the app.

**Where the English comes from.** `scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py:50` sets `LANGUAGE = ''`, which `:1950` turns into `en-US`; `game_language()` (`:308`) only falls back to the game's first language when English is missing. The script has `-l` / `--language` for exactly this (`:1873`), and prints the game's languages while building (`:2106`) — so the information is there, but the GUI never passes the flag. `frontend/Sources/NSPortBuilder/ContentView.swift:1080-1108` assembles:

```
<input dir> -k <keys> --progress json [--env-file <f>] [--work-dir <d>] --platform mac-app -o <out>.app
```

and nothing else. (`--env-file` is only added for `bcOnCPU && target != "mac-app"`, `:1085`, so a Mac app never gets one either — which on its own would have been enough, since `dm/mac/pack_app.py:221` copies it to `Contents/Resources/dm/env.txt`.)

**Why the Launch options sheet does not save it.** Two independent gaps:

1. `LaunchSetting.read` (`frontend/Sources/NSPortBuilder/Library.swift:100-104`) draws that sheet from `Contents/Resources/dm/launcher.json`, and `build_ipa_from_nsp.py` never writes that file. `dm/games/settings.py` — which turns the `DM_LANG` row of `dm/games/settings.tsv:17` into a "Game language" choice — is called only by `dm/ios/tools/build_ipa.sh:98` and `frontend-qt/nspb_qt/win/build_app.py:604`. So a Mac app has no language row at all.
2. Even with the file present, a `launcher.json` row is store-backed, and `Library.swift:184-189` (`launchEnvironment`) deliberately leaves those out of the environment at Play, on the grounds that "the app reads them itself" (`SavedChoices.swift:1-15`, which writes `launcher.<VAR>` into the app's preferences domain). But `dm/mac/launcher.c` in 0.5.0 reads no preferences anywhere: its only `DM_LANG` write is `:202` from `Info.plist`, after the two `env.txt` reads at `:194-195`. The launcher in a 0.5.0 app contains no `launcher.` string at all:

```bash
strings "01008CF01BAAC000.app/Contents/MacOS/nxnative" | grep -c 'launcher\.'   # 0
```

So a choice saved there would be written and then silently ignored.

**What works today** (verified with this build), for anyone who hits this meanwhile:

```
~/Library/Application Support/nxnative/01008CF01BAAC000/env.txt
DM_LANG=zh-Hans
```

The launcher reads that file before `Info.plist`'s `DMLanguage` (`launcher.c:194` before `:202`, both with `if (!getenv(k))`), so it wins, and it survives rebuilds of the app. The log confirms it — `launcher: env DM_LANG=zh-Hans (…)` — and the game comes up in Simplified Chinese (`zh-Hant` for Traditional).

**Suggestions, in the order I would do them**

1. **GUI: a language field or menu at build time, passed as `-l`.** The options are known right after extraction (`nacp.languages(control.nacp)`), and the script already prints them to the build log at `:2106`, so reading them from that line is enough for a first version. This is the one that solves it for players.
2. **`dm/mac/launcher.c`: read `launcher.<VAR>` from the app's preferences domain** for the rows it knows — order env.txt → saved choice → `Info.plist`. As it stands `SavedChoices` is dead code on the C side for every Mac app, not only for language.
3. **`--platform mac-app`: write `dm/launcher.json`** the way `build_ipa.sh:98` does, so the sheet has rows to draw. Only worth doing together with 2.
4. **README `:380`** ("Settings without rebuilding: `Documents/env.txt`") is iOS-only; the Mac's two paths — `~/Library/Application Support/nxnative/<title ID>/env.txt`, then `Contents/Resources/dm/env.txt` — are documented only in `docs/development.md:266`, which is not where a player looks.

Not urgent for me — the `env.txt` above got my game into Chinese. It is the difference, though, between "the Mac version works" and "the Mac version works for anyone who does not read `development.md`".

**Why:** a cold Breath of the Wild build took 53 minutes, and packing the IPA was 10.9 of them: 14.7 GB, nearly all of it the game data (RomFS), written again on every build although it only changes with the game version.

**Upstream:** seedds/nxnative#493 (on top of #478) adds `--romfs separate`. It produces a slim IPA, keeps the image on the Mac (`<id>_build/extract/<version>/RomFS.img`) and writes `romfs.id` into the app. The phone derives the same identity from `Documents/romfs.img` at every start and shows a clear alert when the two don't match. #486 adds DLC from `Documents/aoc`.

**Idea for the installer (Builds → Install on a device):**
- Build with `--romfs separate`.
- Compare the identity of the Mac-side image with the build's `romfs.id` and with what is already on the device. Upload `romfs.img`, and `aoc/` if there is DLC, only when they differ (`devicectl`, as #28 and the Saves sheet do).
- Then install the slim IPA, which takes seconds instead of minutes.
- Say what it does: "Game data is already on the iPhone (1.9.0), installing the app only", or "Uploading game data (14.7 GB) once for this version".

**Waiting on:** #478, #493 and #486 merged and synced into the fork. The identity format is in #493 (`dm/tools/romfs_image.py --identity`).

# iOS build fails: `dm/ios/Sources/main.m` uses `DM_GAME_ID`, which nothing defines

**Title:** iOS build fails with `use of undeclared identifier 'DM_GAME_ID'` (fork patch vs upstream include)

---

## Summary

Building any game for **iOS** (the IPA target) fails at `xcodebuild`. `dm/ios/Sources/main.m` refers to `DM_GAME_ID` in two places, but that macro is only defined in the generated `dm/host/gen/<title ID>/game_profile.h` — a header this file no longer includes. The macOS host and the `mac-app` target are unaffected, because `main.m` is iOS-only.

The failure is **game-independent**: it is not about a particular title, profile or NSP.

## Environment

|          |                                                               |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| macOS    | 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple silicon                                |
| Xcode    | 27.1, iOS SDK 27.1, Metal Toolchain 27.1                      |
| .NET SDK | 10.0.403                                                      |
| Fork     | `main` at commit `1f15ad6`                                    |
| App      | NS Port Builder 0.4.5, **iPhone** target (not Mac app)        |
| Game     | Balatro `0100CD801CE5E000` (v851968) — any game reproduces it |

## Steps to reproduce

1. Pick an NSP folder and `prod.keys` in NS Port Builder.
2. Build the **iPhone** version.

## Actual result

```
[20:45:26] xcodebuild (Release, unsigned, iPhone + iPad)
/Users/…/dm/ios/Sources/main.m:46:40: error: use of undeclared identifier 'DM_GAME_ID'
/Users/…/dm/ios/Sources/main.m:95:35: error: use of undeclared identifier 'DM_GAME_ID'
[20:45:34] FAIL: xcodebuild, log …/ipa/build/ios/pkg/build.log
```

`build.log` shows 179 `CompileC` units with exactly one failure, so everything else compiles.

The two offending lines:

```objc
// line 46, in romfs_locate()
NSString *per_game = [game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID) stringByAppendingPathComponent:@"romfs"];

// line 95, in boot_env()
NSString *gdir = game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID);
```

## Root cause

`DM_GAME_ID` is written by `dm/games/game.py` into the generated profile header:

```
dm/host/gen/0100CD801CE5E000/game_profile.h:3: #define DM_GAME_ID "0100CD801CE5E000"
```

That header reaches the compiler through `-I dm/host/gen/<title ID>`, which is present on the compile line. But the fork's `main.m` no longer includes it — the include was replaced when the file moved to the runtime profile:

```objc
- #include "game_profile.h"   // game profile constants (the RomFS marker path)
+ #include "hle_profile.h"    // the runtime game profile (DM_PROFILE): the RomFS marker path comes from it
```

Upstream `nxnative` still has `#include "game_profile.h"` and never uses `DM_GAME_ID` (it uses `@DM_GAME_ROMFS_MARKER` directly), so upstream is consistent. The inconsistency comes from the fork's patcher, `scripts/sync_upstream.py`, whose `patch_main_m()` injects `game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID)` into both replacement blocks:

- `MAIN_M_ROMFS` → `[game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID) stringByAppendingPathComponent:@"romfs"]`
- `MAIN_M_ENV` → `NSString *gdir = game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID);`

So the patched file references a macro whose defining header the same file no longer includes.

## Suggested fix

**Option A (preferred, what I applied locally):** use the runtime profile for the title ID, exactly as the file already does for the RomFS marker (`dm_profile()->romfs_marker`). No new include needed, and behaviour is identical — without `DM_PROFILE`, `dm_profile()->id` falls back to the compiled macro (`dm/host/hle_profile.c`).

```diff
--- a/dm/ios/Sources/main.m
+++ b/dm/ios/Sources/main.m
@@ -43,7 +43,7 @@ static BOOL romfs_dir_ok(NSString *d) {
-    NSString *per_game = [game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID) stringByAppendingPathComponent:@"romfs"];
+    NSString *per_game = [game_dir_for(dm_profile()->id) stringByAppendingPathComponent:@"romfs"];
@@ -92,7 +92,7 @@ static int boot_env(void) {
-    NSString *gdir = game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID);
+    NSString *gdir = game_dir_for(dm_profile()->id);
```

The same two strings need changing inside `scripts/sync_upstream.py` (`MAIN_M_ROMFS` and `MAIN_M_ENV`), otherwise the next scheduled sync rewrites the bug straight back into `main.m`.

```diff
--- a/scripts/sync_upstream.py
+++ b/scripts/sync_upstream.py
-game_dir_for(DM_GAME_ID)
+game_dir_for(dm_profile()->id)
```

**Option B:** put `#include "game_profile.h"` back into `main.m` next to `hle_profile.h`. Also works — the header is already on the include path — and matches upstream, but leaves the file depending on a compile-time macro while the rest of it uses the runtime profile.

## Verification

- `clang -fsyntax-only` on `dm/ios/Sources/main.m` with the project's own include list and iOS 27.1 SDK: clean.
- Full iPhone build afterwards: `xcodebuild` succeeds, 33 MB IPA produced, `increased-memory-limit` present in the placeholder signature.

## Note on CI

The daily workflow verifies a **macOS host** build, so this iOS-only failure is invisible to it. A `xcodebuild` smoke build for iOS (even `-destination generic/platform=iOS` with signing disabled) would have caught it.
title: iOS build fails with use of undeclared identifier 'DM_GAME_ID' (fork patch vs upstream include)

# `glslangValidator` is required for OpenGL (LÖVE) games but appears in neither the README nor `check_prereqs()`

**Title:** OpenGL games fail at the shader step with no log, because `glslangValidator` is an undeclared dependency

---

## Summary

Building an **OpenGL** game (LÖVE / GLSL titles such as Balatro or Digimon Story Cyber Sleuth) requires `glslangValidator`. It is missing from both places a user would look:

1. the README's dependency line — `brew install xcodegen zstd spirv-cross` — does not mention it;
2. `scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py` → `check_prereqs()`, whose `tools` dict checks `xcodebuild`, `xcodegen`, `dotnet`, `zstd`, `spirv-cross`, `make`, does not mention it either.

The result is a build that runs for many minutes and then dies at the GL shader stage **without writing a log file**, so the GUI shows a failure with nothing to inspect.

## Environment

|          |                                                                          |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| macOS    | 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple silicon                                           |
| Xcode    | 27.1, iOS SDK 27.1, Metal Toolchain 27.1                                 |
| .NET SDK | 10.0.403                                                                 |
| Fork     | `main` at commit `1f15ad6`                                               |
| App      | NS Port Builder 0.4.5, iPhone target                                     |
| Game     | Balatro `0100CD801CE5E000` (v851968, LÖVE 11.4 + OpenGL 4.5 through EGL) |

## Actual result

Everything before the shader stage succeeds:

```
logs/nx_extract_build.log    Build succeeded
logs/rewrite_main.log        main {…} patch 391560
logs/rewrite_sdk.log         sdk  {…} patch 595936
logs/mac_host_build.log      249 lines, warnings only (tools/dmhost produced)
logs/gl_capture.log          35 GLSL shaders captured, "received SIGTERM: graceful exit"
logs/gl_shaders.log          <-- does not exist
```

Then the build stops. The absence of `gl_shaders.log` is the tell: `build_gl_shaders()` checks for the tool **before** `layer_shaders()` creates that log.

```python
def build_gl_shaders(py, repo, roots, sh, env, logs, g, reuse=True, mac=False, provisional=False):
    PROG.stage('GL shaders', step='checking the inputs')
    if not shutil.which('glslangValidator', path=env['PATH']):
        raise BuildError('glslangValidator not found (brew install glslang): it compiles an OpenGL game\'s GLSL shaders')
```

`brew install glslang` fixes it immediately: the same build then reports

```
macosx:   35 shaders (15 vertex) → shader/gl/gl_shaders.metallib
iphoneos: 35 shaders (15 vertex) → shader/ios/gl/gl_shaders.metallib
```

## Suggested fix

**1. `check_prereqs()`** — add the tool so the failure surfaces in the first second instead of after the extraction, rewrite, host build and shader capture:

```diff
-    tools = {'xcodebuild': 'Xcode', 'xcodegen': 'brew install xcodegen', 'dotnet': '.NET SDK 10', 'zstd': 'brew install zstd', 'spirv-cross': 'brew install spirv-cross', 'make': 'Xcode'}
+    tools = {'xcodebuild': 'Xcode', 'xcodegen': 'brew install xcodegen', 'dotnet': '.NET SDK 10', 'zstd': 'brew install zstd', 'spirv-cross': 'brew install spirv-cross', 'glslangValidator': 'brew install glslang', 'make': 'Xcode'}
```

(If an unconditional check is felt to be too strict for NVN / Vulkan games, gate it the way `glslc` is gated: only when the profile's `graphics` is `gl`.)

**2. README** — `brew install xcodegen zstd spirv-cross glslang`.

**3. Optional, but this is what made it hard to diagnose** — have the GL shader step write `logs/gl_shaders.log` (even a one-line "not found" note) before raising, so the GUI always leaves a file behind for the failing stage. The same applies to any other stage whose failure can precede its log.

## Scope

Only OpenGL games are affected. NVN titles (most of the profile list) and Vulkan titles (Hades II) never call `glslangValidator`, so their builds are unaffected — which is probably why this stayed unnoticed.

## Verified

On this machine, installing `glslang 16.6.0` (with `spirv-headers` / `spirv-tools`) and re-running the pipeline carried the same build through to a working 33 MB IPA, and the resulting Mac app boots and plays (3,900 frames, 0 `[RED]` warnings, 614 MB peak memory).
title: OpenGL games fail at the shader step with no log, because glslangValidator is an undeclared dependency

The Mac app fails on any game folder that holds more than one game, with an error that reads like a bug in the build rather than in the folder layout.

**What happens.** The launcher passes the game's folder as the script's input (`ContentView.swift:716`, `args = [… script, inputDir, …]`). The script refuses a folder with more than one title family:

```
scripts/build_ipa_from_nsp.py:454
    if len(fams) > 1: raise BuildError('more than one game in the folder, keep one game per folder: ' + …)
```

That is the right rule for the script — the update and add-on content are matched to the base game by title ID inside one folder, and two families make that ambiguous. But the app never explains it, so a user with a `~/ROMs` folder of five games picks their base `.nsp` from the file picker, presses Build, and gets an error about the folder they were never asked about.

**Why it matters more now.** PR #28 (just merged) makes the launcher install straight to a paired iPhone, which invites exactly this workflow — keep the dumps in one place, build several of them in a row.

**What ufooer did about it** in PR #31, and why the fix is not simply applying that commit: the picked files are staged into a temporary folder whenever the folder holds other games, together with that game's own update and DLC found by title ID. That is the right shape, but it was one commit with two unrelated things (Rosetta detection, which is now on `main` as its own patcher entry, and a 390-line install script that PR #28's Xcode route supersedes), so it could not be taken as-is.

**The fix, as a separate change:**

1. In `BuildModel`, before the build starts: if `inputDir` holds more than one title family, stage the picked base / update / DLC files into a temp folder named after the title ID, and pass that instead.
2. Match update and DLC by title ID prefix, not by "the other files in the folder" — `0100XXXXXXXXX000` and its `0100XXXXXXXXX800` update and `0100XXXXXXXXX001`… add-on content.
3. Say it in the log (`staged 3 files for 0100… into <tmp>: the folder holds 4 games`), so the step is visible rather than magic.

Worth doing before the next release: it is the difference between "the app cannot build from my ROMs folder" and "the app builds whichever game I pick".
title: The Mac app cannot build from a folder that holds more than one game, and does not say why
